cards.s: Fifteen senior questions, with model answers
cards.html:
Practise these aloud; reading is not enough. Each answer is a skeleton, so fill it with your project's details.

1 · How do you decide between continuous delivery and continuous deployment for a model?

It depends on reversibility, blast radius, how fast I learn that a change is wrong, and regulatory oversight. Fast labels, canary analysis and automatic rollback make continuous deployment safe; slow labels and credit decisions argue for a human approval. I'd also split by change type: code-only fixes can flow automatically while new models need approval.

2 · Your metric gate is flaky, and the team wants to remove it. What do you do?

cards.s: Fifteen senior questions, with model answers
cards.html:
First measure: retrain several times and see how much the metric moves without a real change. If the tolerance is inside the noise, the gate is wrong, not the idea. Meanwhile make it a warning, not a blocker, with an owner and a date. Then fix the seeds and the split, set the tolerance from the measured variance, and consider a paired comparison on the same rows. Never widen it silently.

3 · How do you roll back a model when the feature schema changed?

cards.s: Fifteen senior questions, with model answers
cards.html:
Avoid needing to: expand/contract. The new service version accepts both schemas; clients move over; only then is the old field removed. If the model is baked into the image, rolling back the image restores code and model together. With a registry, roll back alias and image. Feature pipelines need the same discipline, or yesterday's model meets today's features.

4 · CI takes 40 minutes. How do you get it under 10?

cards.s: Fifteen senior questions, with model answers
cards.html:
Measure first: which jobs are on the critical path (--durations, job timings). Then, in order of value: parallelise independent jobs, cache dependencies, cancel outdated runs, run only affected tests in a monorepo, move slow integration and full-data training to merge or nightly, and use larger runners for the critical path when cheaper than engineers waiting. Track the p50 and p90 as a team metric.

5 · How do you stop a compromised GitHub Action from reaching production?

cards.s: Fifteen senior questions, with model answers
cards.html:
Pin third-party actions by full commit SHA, with Dependabot to update them; least-privilege permissions per job; no long-lived cloud keys (OIDC, roles that trust specific environments and workflows); production deploys only images built by the trusted workflow, signed and verified by digest; environments with required reviewers; and never run untrusted PR code with secrets (pull_request_target).

6 · What is your testing strategy for an LLM feature?

cards.s: Fifteen senior questions, with model answers
cards.html:
Layers: deterministic unit tests with fakes for chunking, prompts and parsing; integration tests against a real vector store; a golden set for retrieval metrics as the hard gate; LLM-judged faithfulness on a sample, advisory on PRs and hard nightly; cost caps and caching; production feedback flows back into the golden set; a held-out set to detect overfitting to the golden set.

7 · How do you know a deployed model is still good when labels take months?

Proxies: prediction distribution, share of unknown categories, input drift against training data, and business signals like manual override rates. A post-deploy distribution check catches gross errors immediately. Real performance is computed when labels mature, and that job's result can trigger retraining or an investigation.

cards.s: Fifteen senior questions, with model answers
cards.html:
8 · Walk me through an incident you handled.

Use the game day from Chapter 7, in STAR form, and say clearly that it was a planned exercise in a personal project. Detection, timeline, root cause, contributing factors, the action items, and what you changed in the system afterwards.

9 · How would you introduce CI/CD in a team that has none?

Start with the highest-value, lowest-friction step: tests and lint on PRs, required but fast. Then protect main, then automate deploys to staging, then production with approval. Show one metric improving (fewer hotfixes, faster reviews). Pair with the team; don't impose a framework in a big-bang PR.

10 · Monorepo or one repo per model?

cards.s: Fifteen senior questions, with model answers
cards.html:
Monorepo: shared code and atomic changes across services, but needs tooling to build and test only what changed, and ownership via CODEOWNERS. Polyrepo: simple pipelines and clear ownership, but shared code needs versioned packages. With ten teams and a shared feature library I'd lean to a monorepo for libraries and per-service repos for deployables, and say that this is a judgment call.

11 · How do you secure secrets in CI?

Prefer no secrets: OIDC to the cloud. Otherwise environment secrets with reviewers, least scope, rotation, never in logs (masking has limits), no secrets in Dependabot or fork PR runs, push protection and secret scanning on, and a rehearsed process for leaks: rotate first, then clean up.

12 · What would you measure to show the platform works?

cards.s: Fifteen senior questions, with model answers
cards.html:
DORA measures per team, with stability next to speed; adoption of the golden path; time to first deploy for a new service; number of long-lived credentials; CI p90 duration; cost per team. Trends over time, never a league table of teams.

13 · How do you handle a model that is better on average but worse for a group?

Make slices part of the gate, with minimum slice sizes because small slices are noisy. If the trade-off is intentional, it goes through a reviewed baseline change with the reason documented, owned by someone accountable. In a regulated context the slices also belong in the model card.

14 · How do you choose the decision threshold?

cards.s: Fifteen senior questions, with model answers
cards.html:
Not 0.5 by default. From the costs of errors: in the German Credit data, approving a bad applicant is considered about five times as costly as rejecting a good one, so the threshold that minimises expected cost is far below 0.5. It is a business decision with an owner, versioned, tested, and monitored, because changing it changes every decision.

15 · What would you do differently if you rebuilt your project?

Terraform from day one; separate AWS accounts per environment; the distribution check before I needed it; a shared registry so promotion decides what ships. Have a real answer: interviewers ask this to see whether you learn from your own work.

Watch out: Honesty rules for a portfolio project

cards.s: Fifteen senior questions, with model answers
cards.html: Say "in my project" or "I", never "we" for something you built alone. Distinguish measured ("rollback took 2 minutes in my game day") from designed ("I would add canaries at higher traffic"). Never claim production traffic, users or team results you did not have. Interviewers probe exactly these claims, and one invented number undoes everything else.

cards.s: Your stories: what-ifs you actually lived
cards.html:
"Tell me about a time…" questions need stories, and this book gave you real ones if you did the exercises. Map them before the interview:

QuestionStory from this book (if you ran it)
…you found a serious bug in your own designThe single deploy role that let any branch reach production via staging; split into three roles and branch rules (Chapter 5).
…a test passed but the system was wrongThe threshold game day: 31 tests, gate and smoke test green, decisions wrong (Chapter 7).
…you chose a number based on dataMeasuring split variance before setting the gate tolerance (Chapter 6).
…something worked locally but not in productionThe 127.0.0.1 listen address, or the arm64 image on Fargate (Chapter 5).
…you prevented data lossThe force-push trap and --force-if-includes (Chapter 2).
…you kept costs under controlLLM evaluation with caching, budget caps and running the paid gate only on main and nightly (Chapter 6).

cards.s: Your stories: what-ifs you actually lived
cards.html: Each story: one sentence of situation, one of task, three or four of action (with the trade-off), one of result with a number, one of what you learned. Two minutes, not ten.

cards.s: Turn the repositories into evidence
cards.html: A recruiter spends under a minute on your GitHub, a hiring manager maybe five. The repository must answer "what, why, how well" before they scroll.

cards.s: Turn the repositories into evidence
cards.html:
credit-api/README.md now follows this structure; copy it for rag-api:

  1. One paragraph pitch: what it is and what the project is really about ("how a model gets to production safely").
  2. Architecture: one diagram of the pipeline.
  3. Key decisions: a table, each row linking to an ADR.
  4. Measured: real numbers, each with how it was measured. Leave

<measure> until you have measured; never fill in a guess.

  1. Run it: five commands.
  2. Limitations: honest ones. This section builds more trust than any other.

cards.s: Turn the repositories into evidence
cards.html: An ADR is a one-page note: context, options, decision, consequences, and when to revisit. docs/adr/ contains three (runtime, model in image, continuous delivery with approval). Write at least two more yourself: LLM evaluation as advisory on PRs, and the ECR retention and rollback window. ADRs show the skill interviews test most: deciding under constraints and writing it down.

cards.s: Turn the repositories into evidence
cards.html:
• A three-minute screen recording: break the gate in a PR, show the red check, merge a fix, approve production, roll back by SHA, show

/health change. Link it at the top of the README.

  • One blog post (LinkedIn or dev.to), for example "What retraining a model 20 times taught me about CI metric gates": the variance table, the decision, the code. Specific beats general.
  • CV bullets (Lebenslauf): one line each, verb first, number where you measured one. Examples to adapt honestly:

CV bullets (replace ~values with your own):

• Built CI/CD for an ML credit-risk API (GitHub Actions, Docker,
  AWS ECS): OIDC auth with per-environment roles, staged deploys with
  approval, rollback by image SHA in ~2 min (measured in a game day)

  passing all 31 unit tests, the model gate and the smoke test

  with caching and a budget cap; full nightly run < 0.01 USD

For German applications, a link to GitHub in the CV header is common for engineering roles, and English READMEs are normal in international teams; check each job ad for the language it expects.

Exercise: Rewrite a junior answer

cards.s: Turn the repositories into evidence
cards.html:
Take the old two-minute script from the previous edition: "Every pull request runs ruff, mypy and pytest on two Python versions, with an 80 % coverage floor…". Rewrite its first half using the signals table: one trade-off, one number, one failure.

Exercise: Mock system design

Set a timer for 45 minutes and answer Prompt A (LLM feature with weekly prompt changes) aloud, drawing on paper. Record yourself. Compare with the outline: which clarifying questions did you skip?

Exercise: Fill the Measured table

After deploying credit-api, measure the CI duration (p50 over five runs), merge-to-production time excluding the approval wait, and the rollback time. Put the numbers in the README with how you measured them.

Checkpoint: you should now be able to…

cards.s: Turn the repositories into evidence
cards.html:
• explain the difference between a junior and a senior answer, with examples;
  • run a 45-minute system design for a multi-team ML delivery platform: clarify, design, roll out, name risks;
  • answer the fifteen questions aloud from your own project;
  • tell three STAR stories with numbers, without saying "we";
  • publish a README with decisions, measurements and limitations, plus ADRs, a demo and CV bullets you can defend.
